questions.text: The discount column on the left-hand side of cashbook represents a discount
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Cash Book Structure

A cash book typically has two sides:
• Left-hand side (Debit side): This side records all receipts. It includes money received from debtors, cash sales, and any other receipts.
• Right-hand side (Credit side): This side records all payments. It includes payments to creditors, cash purchases, and other payments.

The discount columns in the cash book record the cash discounts related to transactions. There are two types of discounts:
• Discount Allowed: When a business allows a discount to a customer or debtor for early payment, this is recorded on the left-hand (debit) side of the cash book.
• Discount Received: When a business receives a discount from a supplier or creditor, this is recorded on the right-hand (credit) side of the cash book.

---

Step 2: Analyzing the Left-hand (Debit) Side of the Cash Book

The left-hand side of the cash book records money coming into the business. In the discount column on this side, we record any discounts allowed to debtors. Here’s why:
• If the business receives a payment from a debtor, and the debtor is allowed a discount for early payment, that discount is recorded on the left-hand side.
• This discount reduces the amount the debtor has to pay, and it is recorded as an expense for the business (since the business is allowing the discount).

Therefore, the discount recorded on the left-hand side is always a discount allowed to a debtor.

---

Step 3: Eliminate Incorrect Options
• Received from a creditor: This would be recorded on the right-hand side (credit side), not the left. Hence, this is incorrect.
• Received from a debtor: A discount received would be recorded on the credit side, not the debit side. Hence, this is incorrect.
• Allowed to a creditor: This doesn’t make sense in the context of the left-hand side, since we don’t allow discounts to creditors; we allow discounts to debtors. Hence, this is incorrect.

---

Step 4: Conclusion

The discount column on the left-hand side of the cash book represents a discount allowed to a debtor.

So, the correct answer is:
• Allowed to a debtor

questions.text: The control account is used in facilitating
options: the location of errors in the various accounts
the payment of debts and liabilities of the firm
assets distribution with respect to income
questions.explanation:
A control account is a summary account in the general ledger that consolidates the totals of various individual transactions from subsidiary ledgers. Its primary purpose is to make the accounting system more manageable and reduce the clutter in the general ledger.

Step 1: Understanding the Purpose of a Control Account
• Control accounts are used to maintain accuracy and consistency between the general ledger and subsidiary ledgers.
• The subsidiary ledger contains the detailed breakdown of individual transactions (like accounts receivable or accounts payable), while the control account shows just the totals of these transactions.
• This makes it easier to identify discrepancies or errors without going through every single transaction in detail.

Step 2: Analyzing the Answer Choices
• The location of errors in the various accounts:
This is the correct answer. One of the main reasons for using a control account is to reconcile totals and identify differences between the control account and the subsidiary ledger. If there’s a mismatch, it signals that there is an error, making it easier to find and correct the mistake.
• Up to date bank transactions:
Control accounts don’t specifically deal with bank transactions; they consolidate the totals of subsidiary ledgers like receivables or payables. Bank reconciliation is a separate process.
• The payment of debts and liabilities of the firm:
Control accounts are not used for paying debts or liabilities directly; they help in summarizing data like total accounts payable, but not in the actual payment process.
• Assets distribution with respect to income:
This doesn’t relate to the purpose of control accounts. Assets distribution typically falls under broader financial management.

Step 3: Conclusion

The correct answer is the location of errors in the various accounts.

Control accounts help facilitate the identification of errors by reconciling totals between the general ledger and subsidiary ledgers.

The Sales Ledger Control Account (also known as the Debtors Control Account) is a summary account that reflects the total balances of individual customer (debtor) accounts found in the Sales Ledger. It shows the total amount that all customers owe to the business.

Step 1: Understanding the Sales Ledger Control Account
• The Sales Ledger is a subsidiary ledger that contains detailed individual accounts for each customer, showing how much each one owes to the business.
• The Sales Ledger Control Account in the general ledger represents the total of all these individual customer (debtor) balances, summarizing the outstanding debts owed by all customers.

Step 2: Analyzing the Answer Choices

1. The total debtors' account:
• This is the correct answer. The sales ledger control account is the total of all the individual customer accounts (debtors), showing how much is owed to the business.

2. The total creditors' account:
• This is incorrect because creditors represent amounts the business owes to suppliers, and those balances are recorded in the Purchase Ledger Control Account (or Creditors Control Account), not the sales ledger.

3. All day books:
• While the day books (e.g., sales day book) record individual transactions, the sales ledger control account only reflects the debtors' accounts and not all day book entries.

4. Both the debtors' and creditors' accounts:
• This is incorrect because the sales ledger control account only deals with debtors' accounts (customers who owe the business), not creditors' accounts.

Step 3: Conclusion

The correct answer is the total debtors' account because the value of the sales ledger control account is derived from the total of all amounts owed by the customers, which is reflected in the debtors' accounts.

Thus, the correct answer is the total debtors' account.

questions.text: A discount that is allowed to encourage a debtor to pay off his debt within a period is the
questions.explanation:

Explanation:

A cash discount is a reduction in the amount a debtor owes if they pay their debt within a specified short period, typically offered as an incentive for prompt payment. It is often expressed as a percentage of the total debt.

1. Cash Discount:
• A cash discount is offered to customers to encourage them to pay quickly, usually within a specified period (e.g., "2/10, net 30" means a 2% discount is given if the debt is paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days).

2. Annual Discount:

3. Trade Discount:
• A trade discount is a reduction in price given by the seller to a buyer at the point of sale, typically for bulk purchases or as a standard business practice. It does not depend on the timing of the payment.
• Incorrect.

4. Periodic Discount:
• This term is not commonly used in accounting in the context of encouraging quick payment. Discounts are usually referred to by their purpose (e.g., cash discount) rather than their frequency.
• Incorrect.

Conclusion:

The correct answer is cash discount, as it is specifically intended to encourage prompt payment of debts.

questions.text: The book value per share is obtained by dividing?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is shareholders equity by outstanding shares.

Explanation:

The book value per share represents the per-share value of a company's equity, essentially what each share would be worth if the company were liquidated at its current balance sheet value. It is calculated using the following formula:

Book Value Per Share = (Shareholders' Equity)/(Number of Outstanding Shares)

Step 1: Understanding Shareholders' Equity
Shareholders' equity (also known as owners' equity) represents the net assets of the company. It is calculated as:

Shareholders' Equity = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

Shareholders' equity represents the residual interest in the assets of the company after deducting liabilities. It's the value that belongs to the shareholders.

Step 2: Calculating Book Value Per Share
The book value per share gives investors an idea of the value of a share based on the company’s equity. To calculate it, divide the shareholders' equity by the total number of outstanding shares (the shares currently held by shareholders).

Book Value Per Share = (Total Shareholders' Equity)/(Number of Outstanding Shares)

Step 3: Evaluating Other Options

1. Total assets by outstanding shares:
• This would give an idea of the value of total assets per share, but it wouldn't account for liabilities. Book value focuses on equity, which considers both assets and liabilities.
• Not correct.

2. Gross profit by outstanding shares:
• Gross profit is related to the company’s performance over a period and does not reflect the net assets or shareholders' equity.
• Not correct.

3. Net profit by outstanding shares:
• Net profit per share is a performance metric and is related to earnings per share (EPS), not the book value of a share.
• Not correct.

Step 4: Conclusion
The book value per share is obtained by dividing the shareholders' equity by the number of outstanding shares.

Final Answer: Shareholders' equity by outstanding shares

So, the Paid-Up Capital is ₦80,000.

The correct answer is:
• ₦80,000

questions.text: The founders of a company are?
questions.explanation:
The question asks about the people who found a company. Let’s analyze the options to determine the correct answer.

Step 1: Understanding the Role of Founders

The founders of a company are the individuals who take the initial steps to form the company. They are responsible for setting up the business, arranging the legal documents, and ensuring that the company is legally registered. These individuals are commonly referred to as promoters.

---

Step 2: Analyze Each Option

1. Promoters:
• Explanation: Promoters are the individuals who take the steps to form a company. They are responsible for preparing the initial documents, securing funding, and bringing the company into existence. They often raise capital, create the business plan, and file the necessary legal paperwork for the company’s incorporation.
• Conclusion: Correct—The promoters are the founders of the company.

2. Shareholders:
• Explanation: Shareholders are individuals or entities that own shares in a company. They may or may not have been involved in the formation of the company. Shareholders can be investors who buy into the company after it is formed.
• Conclusion: Not correct—Shareholders are owners of the company’s shares but are not necessarily the founders.

3. Canvassers:
• Explanation: Canvassers are individuals hired to solicit business or gather support, typically through direct marketing. They are not involved in forming or founding a company.
• Conclusion: Not correct—Canvassers are not involved in founding a company.

4. Stakeholders:
• Explanation: Stakeholders are individuals or groups who have an interest in the success of a company. This could include employees, customers, suppliers, investors, and others. While founders are a type of stakeholder, stakeholders is a much broader term that includes people who may not be directly involved in the creation of the company.
• Conclusion: Not correct—Stakeholders can include founders but also many others.

---

Step 3: Conclusion

The founders of a company are referred to as promoters. They are the people who take the necessary steps to bring the company into existence and handle its formation.

Final Answer:
The correct answer is: Promoters.

questions.text: One of the items listed below will not be found in a company’s memorandum and article of association. Which is it?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is:

Bank signatories

Explanation:

A company's Memorandum and Articles of Association are legal documents that outline the constitution and internal rules of the company. Let’s break down what each of these documents typically includes and why bank signatories would not be found in them.

1. Memorandum of Association:
This document outlines the external relationships of the company and includes:
• The name of the company.
• The registered office (location) of the company.
• The company’s objectives or the nature of the business it can conduct.
• Liability of the members (whether the liability is limited or unlimited).
• Capital structure (share capital and the distribution of shares).

2. Articles of Association:
This document defines the internal regulations and operating rules of the company, including:
• The powers and duties of directors.
• Shareholder rights and how meetings are conducted.
• Procedures for issuing shares and dividends.
• Rules regarding the alteration of company objectives.

Step 3: Analyze Each Option

1. Objects and their alteration:
• The objects clause specifies the activities the company is authorized to carry out. If the company needs to change its objectives, the Memorandum outlines how these changes can be made.
• Conclusion: This is found in the Memorandum of Association.

2. Location of business:
• The location or registered office of the company is stated in the Memorandum of Association. This is necessary for legal communication and formal purposes.
• Conclusion: This is found in the Memorandum of Association.

3. Bank signatories:
• The names of people authorized to sign cheques or access bank accounts are not part of the Memorandum or Articles of Association. Bank signatories are an internal operational detail typically found in the company’s board resolutions or internal policies, not legal constitutional documents.
• Conclusion: This is not found in either the Memorandum or Articles of Association.

4. Powers of directors:
• The Articles of Association outline the powers and duties of directors, including how they can manage the company’s affairs and the limitations on their authority.
• Conclusion: This is found in the Articles of Association.

Conclusion:

Bank signatories are not found in a company’s Memorandum and Articles of Association. They are typically set internally through board resolutions or similar operational documents.

Final Answer: Bank signatories.

questions.explanation:
Question:

Which of the following is not a source of income for a non-profit organization?
• Entrance fees
• Subscription/dues
• Ordinary shares
• Donations

Step 1: Understand what a non-profit organization is

A non-profit organization (NPO) is an entity that operates for purposes other than making a profit, such as charity, education, religious, or community service. The main goal of non-profits is to reinvest any surplus back into their mission, rather than distributing profits to shareholders or owners.

Step 2: Analyze each source of income

1. Entrance fees:
• Entrance fees are often charged by non-profit organizations to members or participants who join the organization or attend certain events. Examples include membership fees for clubs or admission fees to fundraising events.
• Conclusion: This is a valid source of income for non-profit organizations.

2. Subscription/dues:
• Subscriptions or dues are regular payments made by members to support the activities of a non-profit organization. For example, members of a professional association or sports club may pay annual dues to support the organization.
• Conclusion: This is a valid source of income for non-profit organizations.

3. Ordinary shares:
• Ordinary shares refer to equity ownership in a company. In the case of for-profit businesses, issuing shares is a common way to raise capital from investors. However, non-profit organizations do not have shareholders and are not designed to generate profits for investors, so they cannot issue ordinary shares.
• Conclusion: This is not a source of income for non-profit organizations.

4. Donations:
• Donations are voluntary contributions made by individuals, companies, or other entities to support a non-profit organization's activities. Donations can be monetary or in the form of goods or services.
• Conclusion: This is a valid source of income for non-profit organizations.

Step 3: Identify the correct option

From the analysis, it is clear that ordinary shares are not a source of income for non-profit organizations, as they cannot issue shares for investment purposes like for-profit businesses.

Conclusion:

The correct answer is Ordinary shares, as non-profit organizations cannot issue shares to raise capital.

Final Answer:
• Ordinary shares

questions.text: The accumulation fund of a non-trading concern can equally be referred to as?
questions.explanation:
Let's break down the question step by step to understand what the Accumulation Fund is in a non-trading concern and which of the given options is the best equivalent.

Step 1: Understanding Non-Trading Concerns
A non-trading concern is a not-for-profit organization, such as a club, charity, or society. These organizations do not operate to earn profits for shareholders, but instead, they aim to achieve specific goals or provide services to their members or society.

In a non-trading concern, the main focus is on surpluses and donations rather than profits. Instead of having share capital, these organizations accumulate funds through contributions, donations, and any excess income over expenses, referred to as surpluses.

Step 2: Understanding the Accumulation Fund
The Accumulation Fund (or General Fund in some cases) is a key element of a non-trading concern's finances. It is essentially the net worth of the organization, which consists of:
• Surpluses from previous years (excess of income over expenses).
• Donations and contributions from members or other sources.
• Any other assets (like equipment or property) minus the liabilities (like debts or expenses owed).

The Accumulation Fund is equivalent to the capital or equity in a for-profit business. It represents the amount that belongs to the organization’s members after all liabilities are deducted from the total assets.

Step 3: Analyzing Each Option

Let’s now look at the provided options to understand which one corresponds to the Accumulation Fund:

1. Members' Equity:
• This is the correct answer. Members' Equity refers to the members' stake in the net assets of the organization. In a non-trading concern, the Accumulation Fund serves the same purpose as equity in a for-profit business, representing the total assets minus liabilities. It reflects the organization's value after settling all debts and obligations, and it's essentially the members' interest in the net worth of the organization.

2. Share Capital:
• This is incorrect because share capital applies to for-profit companies that issue shares to raise funds. Non-trading concerns do not have shares or shareholders, so there is no share capital in such organizations.

3. General Fund:
• While some organizations may refer to their Accumulation Fund as the General Fund, this is not as precise a term. The General Fund typically refers to a pool of money used for general operating purposes but does not necessarily represent the total net worth (equity) of the organization.

4. Surplus Fund:
• This is also incorrect because a Surplus Fund refers to excess income over expenses in a single period, which contributes to the Accumulation Fund. However, the Surplus Fund is just one part of the broader Accumulation Fund, not the entire fund itself.

Step 4: Conclusion

The Accumulation Fund is essentially the net worth or equity of the non-trading concern. It represents the members' ownership of the organization’s assets after all liabilities have been settled. Therefore, the best equivalent to the Accumulation Fund is Members' Equity.

Final Answer:
• Members' Equity (Option 1).

questions.text: Which of the following items does not feature in the balance sheet of a club?
options: Salary arrears paid in the current year
Advances subscription in respect of a coming year
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Balance Sheet of a Club
A balance sheet is a financial statement that shows the financial position of an entity at a given point in time. For a club or non-profit organization, the balance sheet typically lists assets (what the club owns or is owed), liabilities (what the club owes), and the accumulated fund (similar to equity for non-profits).

Step 2: Clarifying the Items in the Question
Let’s analyze each option one by one to determine whether it appears on the balance sheet of a club.

---

1. Arrears of current year's subscription:
• Explanation: This refers to unpaid membership fees that are due for the current year. The club is owed this money by its members.
• How it appears: Since it represents money that the club is entitled to receive, it would be shown as an asset under "Receivables" on the balance sheet.

Conclusion: This item appears in the balance sheet under assets.

---

2. Salary arrears paid in the current year:
• Explanation: Salary arrears are amounts owed to employees for services rendered in a prior period but paid in the current year. Since they are now paid, they are no longer a liability at the end of the year.
• How it appears: Salary arrears paid in the current year are an expense for the period. Therefore, they would be recorded in the income and expenditure statement, not on the balance sheet, because they no longer exist as a liability at the year-end.

Conclusion: This item does not appear on the balance sheet. It would be included in the income and expenditure statement.

---

3. Rental income received in advance:
• Explanation: This refers to rental income that the club has received for a future period. The club has received the money but hasn't yet provided the services for that period.
• How it appears: Since the club is holding this money for services it must deliver in the future, it is considered a liability (an obligation) until the service is provided. This would be shown as a liability under "Deferred Income" or "Unearned Income."

Conclusion: This item appears on the balance sheet under liabilities.

---

4. Advance subscription in respect of a coming year:
• Explanation: This is similar to the previous item but involves subscriptions (membership fees) received for a future year. The club has received the payment but owes the membership benefits for the coming year.
• How it appears: Since the club owes future services for the advance subscription received, it would also be classified as a liability under "Subscriptions Received in Advance" or "Unearned Income."

Conclusion: This item appears on the balance sheet under liabilities.

---

Step 3: Final Answer

questions.text: In a non-profit making organisation, the excess of Assets over liabilities equals
questions.explanation:
To answer this question, we need to understand the financial terminology used in the context of non-profit organizations.

Step 1: Understand the Key Concepts

1. Non-Profit Organization:
• A non-profit organization (NPO) is an entity that operates for purposes other than making a profit, such as charitable, educational, or social objectives.

2. Assets:
• These are resources owned by the organization that have economic value, such as cash, buildings, and equipment.

3. Liabilities:
• These are the obligations or debts that the organization owes to others, such as loans or accounts payable.

4. Excess of Assets over Liabilities:
• This refers to what remains after all liabilities have been deducted from the assets. In a business (for-profit) context, this would be referred to as "equity" or "capital."

Step 2: Apply the Concepts to a Non-Profit Organization

In a non-profit organization:
• The concept of "capital" as used in for-profit businesses doesn't apply in the same way.
• Instead, the excess of assets over liabilities is referred to as "accumulated funds" or sometimes "net assets".
• Accumulated funds represent the organization's net worth, which includes all donations, grants, and surpluses that haven't been spent.

Step 3: Evaluate the Given Options

Given the options:
• Capital: This term is typically used in for-profit businesses to refer to the owner's equity or investment in the business.
• Capital Employed: This usually refers to the total amount of capital used in a business, including equity and debt.
• Capital Owned: This is another term related to the equity of a business.
• Accumulated Funds: In a non-profit organization, this term refers to the net assets, or the excess of assets over liabilities.

Conclusion

The correct answer is:
• Accumulated Funds

questions.text: In a partnership account, conversation of non-cash assets into cash is referred to as?
questions.explanation:
Let’s break down this question and the answer, "In a partnership account, conversion of non-cash assets into cash is referred to as?" step by step to fully understand why realization is the correct answer.

Step 1: Understand What Non-Cash Assets Are
Non-cash assets are assets that are not in the form of cash but hold value and can be sold or exchanged for cash. Examples of non-cash assets include:
• Inventory
• Equipment
• Buildings
• Vehicles
• Investments

In a partnership, these assets are often part of the business's resources and can be converted into cash when necessary.

Step 2: The Situation Where Non-Cash Assets Are Converted to Cash
There are several scenarios in a partnership where non-cash assets might need to be converted to cash:
• Dissolution of a partnership: When a partnership ends, the business may sell its assets to pay off debts or distribute the remaining cash to partners.
• Sale of an asset: If the business no longer needs an asset (e.g., selling old equipment), the asset is sold, converting it into cash.
• Liquidation: In cases where the business is winding down, assets may be sold to settle outstanding liabilities.

The process of converting these assets into cash is an essential part of winding up a partnership’s affairs.

Step 3: Terminology in Partnership Accounting
• Realization: This is the key term used in accounting to describe the process of turning non-cash assets into cash. When a partnership is dissolved, or assets are sold, the business realizes these assets, meaning it converts them into cash. The cash proceeds can then be used to settle liabilities, distribute profits, or divide assets among the partners.
• Disposal: Disposal is a more general term that refers to the act of getting rid of an asset, which might involve selling it, scrapping it, or giving it away. While disposal can lead to realization (if the asset is sold for cash), the term “realization” more specifically refers to the cash-conversion process.
• Dissolution: Dissolution refers to the process of legally ending the partnership. While dissolution might involve the realization of assets (selling assets to pay off liabilities), it’s the overall process of winding up the partnership, not specifically the conversion of assets into cash.
• Revaluation: Revaluation is an accounting process where the value of an asset is adjusted to reflect its current market value. This adjustment happens on paper and doesn’t involve converting the asset into cash. Therefore, this term is not related to converting assets into cash.

Step 4: Why Realization Is the Correct Term

When non-cash assets are converted into cash in partnership accounts, the process is called realization because:
• The value of the asset is realized or made actual in the form of cash.
• This term is used in accounting to describe the process of selling assets and receiving cash in return.

For example, during the dissolution of a partnership, all non-cash assets are typically realized by selling them, and the resulting cash is used to settle debts and distribute remaining amounts to the partners.

Step 5: Conclusion

The term realization is the appropriate term for the process of converting non-cash assets into cash in a partnership account. This happens during events such as dissolution, liquidation, or the sale of assets, when the partnership converts the value of its non-cash assets into liquid funds.

Final Answer: Realization

questions.text: Which of the following can be used on admission of a new partnership?
questions.explanation:
When a new partner is admitted into a partnership, certain adjustments need to be made to reflect the change in the partnership's structure, particularly with respect to the assets and liabilities. The correct account used during this process is the Revaluation Account.

1. Revaluation Account:
• Purpose: The Revaluation Account is used when a new partner is admitted into the partnership. The partnership’s assets and liabilities are often revalued to reflect their current market value. This ensures that the existing partners are appropriately compensated for any appreciation or depreciation in the value of the partnership's assets before the new partner joins.
• Conclusion: Correct—This is the account used during the admission of a new partner.

2. Profit Account:
• Explanation: The Profit Account (or Profit and Loss Account) is used to track the overall profit or loss generated by the business, but it is not specifically used for the admission of a new partner.
• Conclusion: Not correct—The profit account is unrelated to the admission of a new partner.

3. Capital Account:
• Explanation: The Capital Account is used to track the investments made by the partners. When a new partner is admitted, they will have a capital account, but this is not the main account used for adjustments on admission. The capital account simply tracks each partner's share in the business.
• Conclusion: Not correct—It is involved in tracking capital contributions, but not for revaluing assets and liabilities.

4. Trading Account:
• Explanation: The Trading Account is used to calculate the gross profit or loss by recording the cost of goods sold and sales, but it is not used in the admission of a new partner.
• Conclusion: Not correct—The trading account is not related to partner admission.

---

Final Conclusion:
The correct account used during the admission of a new partner is the Revaluation Account, as it ensures that any changes in the value of the partnership’s assets and liabilities are accounted for before the new partner is admitted.

Final Answer:
The correct answer is: Revaluation Account.

questions.text:
Use the information below to answer question

Jide and Haruna contribute N12000 each as capital and share profit equally. Jide draws N1500 and Haruna N1700 half-yearly. The profit for the year is N10000. Jide receives a salary of N2000.

The balances of current accounts of Jide and Haruna are respectively?
questions.explanation:
To calculate the balances of the current accounts for Jide and Haruna, we need to consider the following:

1. Profit for the year is N10,000, shared equally between the partners.
2. Jide's salary is N2,000, which is paid before dividing the profit.
3. Drawings are made by each partner half-yearly: Jide withdraws N1,500 every six months (total of N3,000 per year), and Haruna withdraws N1,700 every six months (total of N3,400 per year).

Step 1: Start with the Profit for the Year
• The total profit for the year is N10,000.
• Jide receives a salary of N2,000, which is deducted from the profit before sharing the remaining profit.

So, the adjusted profit is:

Adjusted Profit = N10,000 - N2,000 = N8,000

Step 2: Share the Adjusted Profit Between the Partners
Since the profit is shared equally between Jide and Haruna:

Jide's Share = (8,000)/(2) = N4,000

Haruna's Share = (8,000)/(2) = N4,000

Step 3: Calculate Jide's Current Account Balance
• Jide's Drawings: Jide withdraws N1,500 every six months, totaling N3,000 for the year.
• Jide's Salary: Jide also receives a salary of N2,000.
• Jide's Share of Profit: Jide's share of the profit is N4,000.

Now, Jide's current account balance is calculated as:

Jide's Current Account = Jide's Share of Profit + Salary - Drawings

Jide's Current Account = N4,000 + N2,000 - N3,000 = N3,000

Step 4: Calculate Haruna's Current Account Balance
• Haruna's Drawings: Haruna withdraws N1,700 every six months, totaling N3,400 for the year.
• Haruna's Share of Profit: Haruna's share of the profit is N4,000.

Now, Haruna's current account balance is calculated as:

Haruna's Current Account = Haruna's Share of Profit - Drawings

Haruna's Current Account = N4,000 - N3,400 = N600

Final Answer:
The balances of the current accounts of Jide and Haruna are:
• Jide: N3,000
• Haruna: N600

The correct option is:
• N3,000 and N600

questions.text: The movement of goods from head office to a branch is treated in the head office as
questions.explanation:
Question:
The movement of goods from head office to a branch is treated in the head office as:
• Sales
• Issue
• Purchases
• Requisition

Step 1: Understand the scenario

The question is asking how to account for the movement of goods from the head office to a branch. This situation typically occurs in businesses with multiple locations or departments, where goods need to be transferred from one part of the organization (the head office) to another (the branch).
• Head Office: This is the central office of the business, often controlling inventory, sales, and other administrative functions.
• Branch: This is a separate part of the organization that operates under the head office, possibly in a different location. A branch can sell goods but is still a part of the overall business entity.

Step 2: Analyze the movement of goods

When goods move from the head office to a branch, it is important to recognize that this is an internal transfer of goods. There is no external buyer or seller involved because the branch is part of the same organization as the head office. Therefore, it is not considered a "sale" or a "purchase" in the typical accounting sense.

The main point to note is that the head office is issuing goods to one of its branches. The goods remain within the business, just in a different location (from the head office to the branch).

Step 3: Analyze each option

1. Sales:
• Sales typically refer to the transfer of goods to an external customer in exchange for payment. Since the goods are not being sold to an external party but rather transferred within the organization, this is not considered a sale.
• Conclusion: Sales is not the correct answer.

2. Issue:
• Issue refers to the internal transfer or distribution of goods within the business, such as from the head office to a branch. The head office is "issuing" goods to its branch, and this is an internal movement within the same organization. Therefore, this is the correct term to describe the movement of goods from head office to branch.
• Conclusion: Issue is the correct answer.

3. Purchases:
• Purchases refer to buying goods from an external supplier. Since this is an internal transfer of goods between the head office and branch, it does not involve an external transaction. Therefore, it is not a purchase.
• Conclusion: Purchases is not the correct answer.

4. Requisition:
• A requisition refers to a formal request for goods or services within an organization. While the branch may have requested goods from the head office (through a requisition), this term refers to the requesting process, not the actual movement of goods.
• Conclusion: Requisition is not the correct answer.

Step 4: Conclusion

The correct accounting treatment for the movement of goods from the head office to a branch is to record it as an issue. This represents an internal transfer of goods within the same organization, not an external sale or purchase.

Final Answer:
• Issue

questions.explanation:
To calculate the gross profit for Adex Ltd.'s Ede branch, we use the formula:

Gross Profit = Sales - Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)

Step 1: Calculate the Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)
The formula for COGS is:

COGS = Opening Stock + Goods Sent to Branch - Returns to Head Office - Closing Stock

From the information provided:
• Opening Stock (1st January) = N400
• Goods Sent to Branch = N8,000
• Returns to Head Office = N340
• Closing Stock (31st December) = N720

Now, apply the formula:

COGS = N400 + N8,000 - N340 - N720 = N7,340

Step 2: Calculate Gross Profit
The formula for gross profit is:

Gross Profit = Sales - COGS

From the information provided:
• Sales = N9,160

Now, apply the formula:

Gross Profit = N9,160 - N7,340 = N1,820

Step 3: Conclusion
The gross profit carried to the profit and loss account is N1,820.

• N1,820 (Option A)

questions.text: Costs that vary in proportion to the level of production in a manufacturing environment are known as?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is:

Step 1: Understanding Direct Costs
Direct costs are expenses that are directly tied to the level of production or output in a manufacturing environment. These costs increase or decrease in direct proportion to the amount of goods produced. Examples include:
• Direct materials: The raw materials used to make the product.
• Direct labor: The wages of workers who are directly involved in the production process.

Step 2: Why Other Options are Incorrect
• Control costs: This is not a commonly used term in cost accounting, and it doesn't specifically refer to costs that vary with production.
• Overheads: Overheads are indirect costs, which include expenses like rent, utilities, and management salaries. These do not vary directly with the level of production.
• Indirect costs: These are costs that are not directly tied to production, such as overheads (e.g., rent, utilities, administration expenses).

questions.text: To account for expenses paid by head office on behalf of the branch, the branch should___________

questions.explanation:
When the head office pays expenses on behalf of the branch, it essentially creates an obligation or liability for the branch to the head office. To account for this transaction correctly, the branch needs to recognize that the head office has paid an expense on its behalf and adjust its accounts accordingly.

Step 1: Understand the Transaction
• The head office pays an expense on behalf of the branch.
• The branch needs to recognize the expense in its own profit and loss account, as the expense pertains to its operations.
• Simultaneously, the branch must recognize that it owes the head office for this payment, which is reflected in the head office account.

Step 2: Determine the Correct Accounting Entries

1. Debit Profit and Loss Account:
• This entry is made to record the expense in the branch’s financial records, which will reduce the branch’s profit.

2. Credit Head Office Account:
• This entry acknowledges the liability that the branch has to the head office for paying the expense on its behalf. This increases the amount the branch owes to the head office.

Step 3: Conclusion

The correct accounting treatment when the head office pays an expense on behalf of the branch is:
• Debit profit and loss account and credit head office account

This ensures that the expense is recorded in the branch’s accounts and that the liability to the head office is accurately reflected.

So, the correct answer is:
• Debit profit and loss account and credit head office account

questions.text: How much rent is apportioned to department K?
questions.explanation:
Problem Breakdown:

You are asked to calculate the rent apportioned to Department K. The following information is provided:

• Departments: K, L, M
• Each department's floor space (in square meters) is given:
• K: 120 m²
• L: 80 m²
• M: 100 m²

Step 1: Understand the Basis for Rent Apportionment

In this case, the rent is apportioned based on floor space because rent is typically tied to how much space is used by each department. Therefore, we need to calculate the proportion of rent that department K should bear according to its floor space.

Step 2: Calculate the Total Floor Space

First, sum the total floor space of all departments:

Total floor space = 120 (K) + 80 (L) + 100 (M) = 300 square meters

K's proportion of total floor space = 120/300 = 0.4

Step 4: Calculate K’s Share of the Rent

Now, multiply the total rent (N3,000) by department K’s share of the floor space to find how much rent is apportioned to department K:

K's share of rent = 0.4 × 3,000 = N1,200

Conclusion:

The rent apportioned to department K is N1,200, which corresponds to option A.

Final Answer:
• A) N1,200

questions.text: The current growth in the volume of trading and financial dealing in Nigeria is helped by

Question:
"The current growth in the volume of trading and financial dealing in Nigeria is helped by:"
• Increased financial activities
• Government intervention
• Credit as a factor in business
• Payment for goods in cash

Step 1: Understand the Question

The question asks for the factor that primarily helps explain the current growth in the volume of trading and financial dealings in Nigeria. Trading and financial dealings involve activities like buying, selling, investments, and business transactions. The volume of these activities can be influenced by various economic factors.

Step 2: Analyze Each Option

Let's consider each of the provided options and their impact on trading and financial dealings in Nigeria.

1. Increased Financial Activities:
• Increased financial activities generally include:
• The rise of investment opportunities.
• Growth of stock exchanges, banks, and financial institutions.
• Expansion of digital payment platforms (like mobile banking and fintech companies).
• Greater participation in international trade.
• Impact: This directly leads to an increase in the volume of trading and financial transactions. With more financial tools available (e.g., online trading platforms, better access to credit), businesses and individuals can engage in more transactions and investments, contributing to economic growth.
• Conclusion: Yes, increased financial activities are a primary factor that helps grow trading and financial dealings.

2. Government Intervention:
• Government intervention can involve policies that regulate the financial sector, protect investors, and ensure market stability. While government policies (like interest rate controls, monetary policy, or trade agreements) can encourage business growth, government intervention alone is not the main driver of growth in trading volume.
• Impact: Government intervention plays a supporting role, but the day-to-day growth in trading is more driven by economic activities and market forces rather than just government policies.
• Conclusion: No, government intervention helps, but it is not the main factor.

3. Credit as a Factor in Business:
• Credit availability enables businesses to access loans and finance for growth. This allows businesses to invest, expand operations, and increase their trading activities.
• Impact: Credit is important for business operations, but credit alone does not fully explain the growth in volume of trading and financial dealings. It's a supporting factor, but not the main driver.
• Conclusion: No, credit is important but not the primary reason for the growth.

4. Payment for Goods in Cash:
• Payment in cash refers to physical currency transactions. In today's world, economies (including Nigeria) are moving toward cashless transactions, which are faster, more efficient, and safer. Relying solely on cash payments can limit growth, especially in larger transactions.
• Impact: Payment in cash is not a significant driver of growth in trading and financial dealings. In fact, electronic payments, credit, and digital platforms are more efficient for handling large volumes of transactions.
• Conclusion: No, payment in cash is not a key driver for the growth in trading volume.

Step 3: Conclusion

From the analysis, it's clear that increased financial activities—including the rise of fintech, digital banking, online trading platforms, and the general expansion of financial services—are the key drivers of growth in the volume of trading and financial dealings in Nigeria.

Final Answer:
• Increased financial activities
• Increased financial activities include the growth of the financial sector, digital platforms, and international trading, all of which directly contribute to increased trading and financial dealings.
• Other options, like government intervention, credit, and cash payments, are supportive factors but not the main cause of the current growth in trading and financial activities.

questions.text: In departmental accounting, which is not a transfer pricing_________
questions.explanation:
To answer the question, let's first understand what transfer pricing is and the common types of transfer pricing methods used in departmental accounting.

Step 1: Understand Transfer Pricing
Transfer pricing refers to the prices at which goods, services, or intangibles are transferred between departments or divisions within the same organization. It is a way of allocating revenue and costs to the various parts of a business. Common methods include:

1. Cost-Based Transfer Price:
• This method sets the transfer price based on the cost of producing the goods or services. It can include just the variable cost, full cost, or cost plus a profit margin.

2. Market-Based Transfer Price:
• This method sets the transfer price based on the market price that the goods or services would fetch if sold to an external customer.

3. Dual Pricing System:
• Under this system, two prices are used: one for the selling department and one for the buying department. This is done to balance the interests of both departments.

Step 2: Identify the Option That Is Not a Transfer Pricing Method

4. Peak Pricing:
• Peak pricing refers to a pricing strategy where prices are higher during periods of high demand (peak periods) and lower during periods of low demand. This is commonly used in industries like utilities, transportation, and hospitality but is not typically a method of transfer pricing within departmental accounting.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct answer is:
• Peak pricing

By maintaining branch accounts at the head office, the organization can:

2. Ensure Consistency and Control: By centralizing the accounting functions, the head office can ensure that all branches follow the same accounting policies and procedures, maintaining consistency across the organization.

3. Consolidate Financial Data: The head office can consolidate financial data from all branches to prepare comprehensive financial statements for the entire organization.

Step 2: Analyze the Given Options

questions.text: The addition of prime cost, indirect cost and opening work-in-progress less the closing work-in-progress will result in cost of
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is goods manufactured.

1. Prime Cost:
• This is the sum of direct materials, direct labor, and direct expenses. It represents the direct costs of production.

2. Indirect Cost:
• These are overhead costs or factory overheads, which include indirect materials, indirect labor, and other factory costs that are not directly attributable to specific units of production.

3. Work-in-Progress (WIP):
• Opening WIP refers to the unfinished goods at the beginning of the period.
• Closing WIP refers to the unfinished goods at the end of the period.

Formula to Calculate the Cost of Goods Manufactured:

Cost of Goods Manufactured = Prime Cost + Indirect Costs (Overhead) + Opening Work-in-Progress - Closing Work-in-Progress

Explanation:
• The prime cost includes all direct costs associated with production.
• The indirect costs (factory overhead) are added to the prime cost to account for the factory overheads incurred during production.
• Opening WIP is added because it's part of the production that carried over from the previous period, while closing WIP is subtracted because it's the part of the current production that is not yet completed by the end of the period.

This formula gives us the cost of goods manufactured, which represents the total cost of all goods completed during the period.

Other Options:
• Goods available for sale: This would include finished goods inventory and is relevant to retail but not directly tied to the manufacturing process.
• Goods sold: This refers to goods that have already been sold, not just manufactured.
• Materials put into production: This refers only to direct materials used in production and doesn't account for labor, overhead, or WIP.

Conclusion:
The addition of prime cost, indirect costs, and opening WIP minus closing WIP gives the cost of goods manufactured.

Final Answer:
The correct answer is goods manufactured.

questions.text: The account of government into which all monies are received and from which all expenditures are disbursed is the
questions.explanation:
The correct answer to this question is the Federation Account.

1. Federation Account:
• The Federation Account is the primary account into which all revenues collected by the federal government of a country are deposited. This includes taxes, royalties, and other income from various sectors such as oil and gas.
• From this account, money is distributed to various levels of government (federal, state, and local) according to a revenue-sharing formula.
• This account is the central pool from which government expenditures are disbursed.

2. Petroleum Technology Development Fund:
• This is a fund specifically set up to develop and promote the education and training of personnel in the oil and gas industry. It is not the central account where all government monies are received and disbursed from.

3. Central Bank Account:
• The Central Bank Account holds the reserves and operational funds for the Central Bank of the country. It is not where all government revenue is pooled for disbursement to other governmental bodies.

4. Development Fund:
• The Development Fund is used for specific projects or initiatives aimed at economic development. It does not serve as the primary account for receiving all government revenue and making expenditures.

Conclusion:
The correct answer is Federation Account. This is the account into which all government revenue is received and from which all government expenditure is made.

questions.text: Cost classification in relation to charges is determined by the level of?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer to the question is:
• Activity

Explanation:

Cost classification in relation to charges refers to how costs are categorized based on different factors within the business. When considering cost classification in relation to charges, one key factor is the level of activity. Here's why:

Step 1: Understand Cost Classification
Costs in a business are typically classified to help understand, manage, and control them better. One of the ways costs can be classified is based on their behavior or their relation to certain levels of business operations (or activity levels).

There are three main types of costs classified by activity:
1. Fixed Costs: These do not change with the level of activity (e.g., rent, insurance).
2. Variable Costs: These vary directly with the level of activity (e.g., raw materials, direct labor).
3. Semi-variable (or Mixed) Costs: These have both fixed and variable components (e.g., utility bills with a fixed service fee and a usage-based component).

Step 2: Relation to Charges and Activity
The "charges" here refer to how costs are allocated or charged based on what the business is doing—whether it's producing goods, offering services, or engaging in other activities. As activity increases or decreases, costs like materials, labor, and utilities will change.
• Raw materials and labor are examples of variable costs that depend on the level of activity.
• Fixed costs, such as rent, may not change with the level of activity but are still related to the overall structure of cost behavior in relation to charges.

Step 3: Why Activity?
Costs are often classified in terms of how they react to changes in the level of activity within the business. This helps managers understand how costs behave and plan accordingly. For example:
• If a company increases production, it will incur more variable costs such as labor and raw materials.
• Conversely, during a period of low activity, these costs will decrease.

Thus, activity is the main factor influencing cost behavior and classification when it comes to charges.

Step 4: Other Options
• Raw materials: This is a specific type of cost (variable cost), not a general classification method.
• Labour: Like raw materials, labor is a type of cost, but not the key factor for determining cost classification.
• Profitability: This refers to the overall financial performance but is not directly used in classifying costs in relation to charges.

Thus, activity is the most appropriate factor for cost classification in relation to charges.

questions.text: Which method of pricing can be used satisfactorily in either a rising or falling price situation?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is:
• Average method

Step 1: Understanding the Average Method
The average method (also known as the weighted average cost method) calculates the cost of inventory by averaging the cost of all similar goods available during the period. It smooths out price fluctuations, whether prices are rising or falling, by using the average cost of all units for pricing inventory and cost of goods sold.

Step 2: Why the Average Method Works in Both Rising and Falling Price Situations
In both rising and falling price environments, the average method provides a stable and consistent valuation because it spreads the cost of goods evenly across all units, avoiding the extremes of high and low prices.

Step 3: Why Other Options are Incorrect
• Standard price: This is a predetermined cost set by the company, and it may not reflect current market conditions, especially in rising or falling price situations.
• Marketing price: This refers to pricing strategies for selling goods and does not relate to inventory valuation methods.
• FIFO (First-In, First-Out): FIFO assumes that the oldest inventory is sold first. In a rising price situation, it will lead to lower cost of goods sold (and higher profits), while in a falling price situation, it will lead to higher cost of goods sold (and lower profits). Thus, it is not as neutral as the average method.

Step 4: Conclusion
The average method is best suited for both rising and falling price situations because it evens out the price fluctuations.

Thus, the correct answer is:
• Average method (Option D)

questions.explanation:
To determine the cost of goods credited to the head office trading account, we need to calculate the cost of goods sent by the head office and adjust it for goods returned to the head office and the change in stock. This can be done using the formula for the cost of goods sold (COGS):

COGS = Opening Stock + Goods Received - Goods Returned - Closing Stock

Step 1: Identifying the relevant data

• Goods received from the head office: N800,000
• Goods returned to the head office: N34,000

• Sales: N916,000 (Sales are not used directly in calculating the cost of goods credited to the head office trading account.)

Step 2: Apply the formula
Now we will calculate the cost of goods credited to the head office trading account (COGS):

COGS = Opening Stock + Goods Received - Goods Returned - Closing Stock

Substitute the values:

COGS = 40,000 + 800,000 - 34,000 - 72,000

COGS = 840,000 - 106,000

COGS = N734,000

Final Answer: N734,000

questions.text: Given that 1/3 of the N6000 stock held by a branch is purchased from outsiders. If goods are invoiced to branch at 25% on cost, the provision for unrealized profit is?

To calculate the provision for unrealized profit, follow these steps:

We are told that 1/3 of the branch's stock is purchased from outsiders, meaning that 2/3 of the stock is purchased from the head office. Therefore, the value of the stock purchased from the head office is:

Step 2: Calculate the Unrealized Profit Percentage
Goods are invoiced to the branch at 25% on cost. This means the profit percentage is 25% of the cost, which we can express as a fraction of the selling price:

The provision for unrealized profit is calculated as 20% of the stock purchased from the head office (N4,000):

Provision for Unrealized Profit = 0.20 × N4,000 = N800

The provision for unrealized profit is N800.

Thus, the correct answer is:

questions.text:
Use the information below to answer questions

Jan. 1 Received 1,000 units at N10 each

Jan. 2 Received 2,000 units at N12 each

Jan. 3 Issued 1,500 units

Jan. 4 Received 1,000 units at N11 each

Jan. 5 Issued 1,000 units

What is the value of closing stock using simple average?
questions.explanation:
To solve this question using the Simple Average Method, we need to calculate the average cost per unit of the stock received and then apply this average to the remaining units in inventory (closing stock). Let's break it down step by step:

Step 1: Calculate the Simple Average Price Per Unit
The simple average price per unit is calculated by averaging the prices of the units received on different dates, without weighting by quantity.

Let’s first list the unit prices:
• Jan. 1: 1,000 units at N10 each
• Jan. 2: 2,000 units at N12 each
• Jan. 4: 1,000 units at N11 each

Now calculate the simple average price per unit:

Average Price = (10 + 12 + 11)/(3) = 33/3 = N11

So, the simple average price is N11 per unit.

Step 2: Track the Issued Units and Remaining Stock
Now, we need to determine how many units are left in stock after the issues (using this simple average method).

Initial Purchases:
• Jan. 1: 1,000 units received.
• Jan. 2: 2,000 units received.
• Jan. 4: 1,000 units received.

Total units received = 1,000 + 2,000 + 1,000 = 4,000 units.

Issuance:
• Jan. 3: Issued 1,500 units.
• Jan. 5: Issued 1,000 units.

Total units issued = 1,500 + 1,000 = 2,500 units.

Remaining stock:
• Closing stock = Total units received – Total units issued = 4,000 – 2,500 = 1,500 units.

Step 3: Calculate the Value of the Closing Stock
Now, we multiply the remaining stock by the average price per unit:

Closing Stock Value = 1,500 units × N11 per unit = N16,500

Final Answer:
The value of the closing stock using the simple average method is N16,500, which corresponds to the third option.

Recap:
1. Calculate the simple average price per unit.
2. Track the total units received and issued.
3. Multiply the remaining units by the average price to find the closing stock value.

Answer: N16,500

Balance as per overdraft of the cashbook is ₦4,000
Uncredited cheque is ₦2,300
Bank charges ₦300
Unpresented cheque ₦5,000

What is the adjusted cashbook balance?
questions.explanation:
To calculate the adjusted cashbook balance, we need to take into account the overdraft balance, uncredited cheques, bank charges, and unpresented cheques. Let's break this down step by step.

Step 1: Start with the Cashbook Balance
• Balance as per overdraft in the cashbook: ₦4,000 (This is a negative balance, indicating an overdraft).

Step 2: Adjust for Bank Charges
• Bank charges: ₦300 (Bank charges reduce the cashbook balance).
• Since this is an expense, we subtract it from the cashbook balance.

Adjusted Cashbook Balance = ₦4,000 + ₦300 = ₦4,300 overdraft (increased debt)

Step 3: Consider Uncredited Cheques
• Uncredited cheques: ₦2,300
• Uncredited cheques are amounts that have been recorded in the cashbook but not yet processed by the bank. Since this has not been credited by the bank, it does not affect the cashbook balance directly.

Step 4: Consider Unpresented Cheques
• Unpresented cheques: ₦5,000
• Unpresented cheques are amounts written by the company that have not yet been cleared by the bank. These cheques would still be shown in the cashbook, but they have not yet been processed by the bank, so they don't affect the cashbook balance directly.

Step 5: Calculate the Adjusted Cashbook Balance
Considering the above points:
• Overdraft balance: ₦4,000
• Plus bank charges: ₦300

The adjusted cashbook balance is:

Adjusted Cashbook Balance = ₦4,000 + ₦300 = ₦4,300 overdraft (meaning more is owed)

Conclusion:
The correct answer is:
• ₦4,300 (overdraft).

questions.text: When a bill is negotiated to a bank, it is said be?
questions.explanation:
Question:
_When a bill is negotiated to a bank, it is said to be:_
1. Surrendered
2. Cashed
3. Discounted
4. Accepted

Step 1: Understand What it Means to Negotiate a Bill

A bill of exchange is a financial instrument that orders one party to pay a fixed amount of money to another party at a predetermined future date.

When the holder of a bill needs immediate cash, but the bill is not due for payment yet (before its maturity date), they can present the bill to a bank. This process is known as negotiating the bill to the bank.

Step 2: What Happens When a Bill is Negotiated to a Bank

When the bill is presented to the bank:
1. The bank pays the holder of the bill an amount that is less than the face value of the bill.
2. The bank deducts a discount (interest) based on the remaining time before the bill reaches its maturity date.
3. The bank will then collect the full value of the bill from the drawee (the person who has to pay) when the bill matures.

This process is known as bill discounting.

Step 3: Review the Provided Options

1. Surrendered: This would imply giving up a document or rights, but it's not specific to the financial transaction involving a bill.

2. Cashed: This term refers to converting a check or other instrument into cash, but doesn’t capture the idea of the bank deducting a discount for early payment.

3. Discounted: This is the correct term used when a bill is presented to a bank and exchanged for cash, with the bank deducting a fee or discount based on the remaining time until maturity.

4. Accepted: Acceptance is a different concept in bills of exchange. It refers to when the drawee formally agrees to pay the bill at maturity, not when the bill is negotiated with a bank.

Step 4: Conclusion

The correct answer is discounted, because when a bill is negotiated to a bank, the bank discounts the bill by paying the holder less than the bill's full value. The difference is the bank's fee for providing early payment.

questions.text:
Show how the following transaction will be recorded applying the double entry principle:

Rent ₦50,000 was paid by Mr. Roi to his landlord on 1st July, 20 × 7 by cheque.
options: Dr Rent A/c; Dr Bank A/c
Dr Bank A/c; Cr Rent A/c
Dr Rent A/c; Cr Bank A/c
Dr Rent A/c; Cr Mr. Roi
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the Transaction
• Transaction Details:
• Rent Paid: ₦50,000
• Paid By: Mr. Roi
• Paid To: His landlord
• Payment Method: By cheque
• Date: 1st July, 20×7

Step 2: Identify the Accounts Involved

In this transaction, two accounts are involved:

1. Rent Account: This account represents the expense incurred by Mr. Roi for rent.
2. Bank Account: This account represents the cash or funds held by Mr. Roi in his bank.

Step 3: Determine the Effect on Each Account

According to the double entry principle:
• Rent Account (Expense Account):
• When rent is paid, it is an expense for Mr. Roi. Expenses increase on the debit side.
• Therefore, the Rent Account will be debited.
• Bank Account (Asset Account):
• When Mr. Roi pays the rent by cheque, money is leaving his bank account. A decrease in an asset account (like cash or bank) is recorded on the credit side.
• Therefore, the Bank Account will be credited.

Step 4: Applying the Double Entry Principle

Based on the analysis:
• Debit: Rent Account (Dr Rent A/c) → This reflects the increase in the rent expense.
• Credit: Bank Account (Cr Bank A/c) → This reflects the decrease in the bank balance due to payment.

Step 5: Conclusion

The correct way to record this transaction using the double entry principle is:
• Dr Rent A/c; Cr Bank A/c

So, the correct option is:
• Dr Rent A/c; Cr Bank A/c

questions.text: Which of the following is used to update the cash book in bank reconciliation?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is:
• Interest received and direct credit

Step 1: Understanding Bank Reconciliation
Bank reconciliation is the process of comparing the cash book (the company's record of its bank account) with the bank statement to ensure that all transactions are accounted for and that the balances match.

There are some transactions recorded by the bank that the company might not be immediately aware of, such as interest received, direct credits, bank charges, and direct debits. These need to be updated in the cash book.

Step 2: Why "Interest Received and Direct Credit" is Correct
• Interest received: Banks sometimes credit interest to a business's account. This might not be recorded in the company's cash book until the business becomes aware of it. To reconcile the cash book, this interest must be added.
• Direct credit: This refers to payments or transfers made directly into the business's bank account by third parties (customers, clients, etc.). These may not be recorded in the company's cash book until they are noticed during the bank reconciliation process.

Step 3: Why Other Options are Incorrect
• Interest received and unpresented cheques: While interest received is correct, unpresented cheques are cheques issued by the company but not yet cashed or cleared by the bank. These don't affect the cash book update directly; they are used to adjust the bank reconciliation statement instead.
• Commission and debit note: Commission could be a bank charge, but debit notes are documents that indicate adjustments in accounts payable and do not update the cash book directly.
• Unpresented cheques and direct credit: Unpresented cheques are not used to update the cash book; they are used to reconcile the bank statement. Direct credits, however, do affect the cash book, so this option is only half correct.

Step 4: Conclusion

To update the cash book in bank reconciliation, you need to account for transactions like interest received and direct credits. These are transactions recorded by the bank that the company might not have recorded yet.

Thus, the correct answer is:
• Interest received and direct credit

questions.text: The bank charges levied on a current account holder is the charge on?
questions.explanation:
The question asks about the bank charges levied on a current account holder, which refers to the specific fees that the bank imposes for maintaining and using the account.

Step 1: Understanding Bank Charges on Current Accounts

Banks typically levy charges on current account holders for a variety of services, such as maintaining the account, processing transactions, and providing other banking services. The charge that is most commonly applied to a current account holder is based on the total value of transactions carried out during a specific period.

Step 2: Analyze Each Option

1. Transaction:
• Explanation: Banks may charge for certain individual transactions (such as processing checks, withdrawals, or electronic transfers), but this is typically not the main fee applied to current account holders.
• Conclusion: Not the most common charge—Banks may charge for specific transactions, but this is not the main type of charge applied to the overall account.

2. Turnover:
• Explanation: Turnover charges refer to fees based on the total value of transactions (both deposits and withdrawals) made in the current account over a specific period. This is a common method banks use to calculate charges for account holders. The fee is usually a percentage of the account's turnover.
• Conclusion: Correct—Turnover charges are typically levied on current account holders based on the total value of transactions over a period.

3. Transfer:
• Explanation: Banks may charge for fund transfers (for example, transferring money between accounts), but this is not the primary charge levied on a current account holder. Transfer fees are usually one-off fees for specific transactions.
• Conclusion: Not correct—Transfer charges apply to specific transactions, not the overall charge on a current account.

4. Cash Received:
• Explanation: Banks typically do not levy charges based on the amount of cash received into an account. Cash receipts are part of the turnover but are not the basis for a bank charge by themselves.
• Conclusion: Not correct—Cash received is part of the account activity, but banks usually do not charge specifically for this.

---

Step 3: Conclusion

The most common bank charge for a current account holder is based on the turnover of the account, which refers to the total value of transactions carried out during a specified period.

Final Answer:
The correct answer is: Turnover.

questions.text: The most convenient cash book used by a petty trader operating in an area where there is no banking facility is?
questions.explanation:
Let's go through the types of cash books and figure out which one would be most suitable for a petty trader operating in an area where there is no banking facility.

Step 1: Understanding Different Types of Cash Books

1. Four-Column Cash Book: This type of cash book has four columns for recording both cash and bank transactions, with two columns on each side for recording cash and bank payments, and cash and bank receipts. Since it includes bank transactions, it is not useful for someone without access to a bank.

2. Three-Column Cash Book: This type of cash book has three columns for each side (debit and credit) – one for cash transactions, one for bank transactions, and one for discount allowed and received. Again, since it involves bank transactions, it's not suitable for a petty trader with no access to a banking facility.

3. Single-Column Cash Book: This is the simplest form of cash book. It has only one column for cash transactions, meaning it records only cash receipts and cash payments. Since a petty trader in an area without banking facilities will deal primarily with cash transactions, this cash book is simple, convenient, and appropriate for such a trader.

4. Two-Column Cash Book: This type of cash book has two columns on each side – one for cash transactions and one for discounts (both allowed and received). While it can handle discounts, it still focuses mainly on cash transactions, making it somewhat more advanced but still appropriate for someone who primarily deals with cash.

Step 2: Choosing the Most Convenient Option
Given that the trader has no access to banking facilities, the Single-Column Cash Book is the most convenient option. It’s simple, easy to use, and only tracks cash payments and receipts, which is ideal for a petty trader operating in a cash-only environment.

Final Answer:
• Single column (Option 3).

questions.text: Recurrent expenditure are expenses for the period not exceeding?
questions.explanation:
Recurrent expenditure refers to the ongoing, regular expenses necessary for the day-to-day functioning of the government or an organization. These include costs such as salaries, utility bills, maintenance, and supplies. Unlike capital expenditures, which are for long-term investments, recurrent expenditures are shorter-term, recurring costs.

Step 1: Understanding the Time Frame of Recurrent Expenditure
Recurrent expenditures are incurred on a yearly basis and are part of the annual budget. These expenses are necessary to maintain the regular operations of a government or business for a single fiscal year. Recurrent expenditures do not extend beyond the current year, as they are planned and budgeted to be recurring annually.

Step 2: Analyzing the Time Frame in the Options
The question asks for the period that recurrent expenditures do not exceed:

1. 10 years: This is too long for recurrent expenditure. It relates more to long-term capital investments.

2. 5 years: While shorter than 10 years, this is still too long for recurrent expenditure, which focuses on immediate, ongoing operational needs.

3. 2 years: This is closer but still too long, as recurrent expenses are budgeted annually.

4. 1 year: This is the correct answer, as recurrent expenditures are planned for and incurred within a fiscal year (12 months).

Final Answer:
• 1 year (Option 4).

2. ii) Cash in hand:

3. iii) Premises:

Step 1: Understand What Directors' Salaries Are

Directors' salaries are payments made to the directors of a company for their services. These are part of the operating expenses of a company, similar to the way employee salaries or other administrative expenses are categorized.

Step 2: Identify Which Financial Statement Tracks Salaries and Other Expenses

To answer the question correctly, we need to figure out where salaries, including directors' salaries, are recorded. There are a few key financial statements in accounting, each serving a specific purpose. Let's review each option:

1. Current Liabilities:
• These are obligations that a company must settle within a year, like trade payables or short-term debt.
• Directors' salaries are not liabilities; they are expenses, so this option is incorrect.

2. Profit and Loss Account (Income Statement):
• This financial statement records all revenues and expenses over a period, summarizing the company's performance in terms of profit or loss.
• Directors' salaries are an expense, and expenses are recorded in the profit and loss account. This is the correct option.

3. Trading Account:
• The trading account is concerned with gross profit, i.e., sales minus the cost of goods sold (COGS). It doesn't account for operational or administrative expenses, like salaries.
• Since directors' salaries are part of administrative expenses and not directly tied to the cost of goods, this is not the right answer.

4. Current Account:
• In accounting, a current account typically refers to the capital accounts in partnerships or the bank account used for day-to-day operations. This is unrelated to salary expenses.
• Directors' salaries are not part of a current account, so this option is incorrect.

Step 3: Eliminate Incorrect Options

Based on the explanation:
• Current liabilities are debts/obligations, not salaries.
• Trading account is for calculating gross profit and doesn’t involve expenses like salaries.
• Current account in this context is irrelevant.

Step 4: Confirm the Correct Answer

Salaries, including directors' salaries, are classified as an expense in the Profit and Loss Account (P&L account) because they reduce the company's profit for the period.

Therefore, the correct answer is:
• Profit and Loss Account

Summary:

When the company pays directors' salaries, this is treated as an expense. All expenses (like salaries, rent, utilities, etc.) are recorded in the profit and loss account. These expenses reduce the company’s profits, and that’s why they are tracked in this financial statement.

If you have further questions or need clarification on this topic, feel free to ask!
